question.problem:
Using the definition of the hyperbolic cosine, calculate ${f}^{-1}(x)$ given that $f(x)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2x-3)$ and $x\ge \frac{3}{2}.$

${f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡($
{{field-1}}$)+$
{{field-2}}
question.worked_solution:
Let $y=\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2x-3).$ Since $x\ge \frac{3}{2},$ we have $y\ge 1.$

To find the inverse function, we swap $x$ and $y:$

$$
x=\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2y-3),
$$

where $x\ge 1$ and $y\ge \frac{3}{2}.$

Next, we apply the definition of hyperbolic cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}\,({e}^{2y-3}+{e}^{-(2y-3)}) \\ 2x & ={e}^{2y-3}+{e}^{-(2y-3)} \\ 2x{e}^{2y-3} & ={e}^{4y-6}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Bringing everything to the left-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{4y-6}-2x{e}^{2y-3}+1 & =0 \\ ({e}^{2y-3})^{2}-2x({e}^{2y-3})+1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $Y={e}^{2y-3}.$ We can form a quadratic equation in $Y$ and solve it by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Y}^{2}-2xY+1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2}-{x}^{2}+1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ Y-x & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ Y & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ {e}^{2y-3} & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ 2y-3 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Note that for  $x\ge 1,$ we have $x-\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\le 1$ and  $x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\ge 1.$ Since $2y-3\ge 0,$ the logarithm in the above equality must be positive, so we reject the alternative with the negative sign. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2y-3 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}) \\ y & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})+3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 Therefore,

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})+\frac{3}{2}.
$$
